pinterest.title: Armenian Wedding Traditions in Order: From Khosk-Kap to Kochari
pinterest.description: Armenian wedding traditions are rarely a single day. Follow them in the order families live them: the formal asking (khosk-kap), the engagement, choosing the kavor and kavorkin, the church crowning, lavash, honey and a plate at the groom's door, then the duduk and Kochari. We note which details come from UNESCO, the Smithsonian or parish sources and which are simply often told. Your own family's version is the one that counts.

pinterest.title: The Armenian Church Wedding: What the Crowning and Shared Cup Mean
pinterest.description: Parishes describe the crowning as the high point of an Armenian Apostolic wedding. The crowns stand for the glory and honour with which God crowns the couple, as king and queen of their own home, and the couple drink from a blessed cup as a sign they will share everything in life, joys and sorrows alike. Practice can vary, so ask your priest. A guide to Armenian wedding traditions.

pinterest.title: Lavash, Honey and a Broken Plate: Armenian Wedding Customs at the Door
pinterest.description: UNESCO records that lavash is placed on the shoulders of newlyweds to bring fertility and prosperity. In the Smithsonian's account, the mother-in-law lays it there and offers the couple honey and walnuts as they enter the groom's house, and the couple break plates to cast off evil. By tradition, whoever breaks a plate first takes charge of the household. More Armenian wedding traditions inside.

slides: Armenian wedding traditions you did not know: an Armenian wedding is rarely a single day.
It starts with khosk-kap, the formal asking. Families often tell of a pause before the yes, which some say makes the answer a shared decision.
The kavor and kavorkin are the couple's wedding godparents and sponsors for life. Families usually tell it this way, so ask your parish about the kavor's role.
Parishes describe the crowning as the high point of the service. The couple are crowned as king and queen of their own home and share a blessed cup.
At the groom's door: lavash on the couple's shoulders for fertility and prosperity (UNESCO), a spoonful of honey and walnuts, and plates broken to cast off evil.
Then the music. Duduk music is usually played by two musicians, one holding a continuous drone while the other carries the melody.
Kochari is the group dance UNESCO inscribed in 2017, open to everyone whatever their age. Grandparents and school friends end up in the same line.
Every family keeps its own version. Planning around yours, at home or abroad? Start a conversation with a Wedded Advisor.

An Armenian wedding is rarely a single day. It is a run of family moments, from a formal visit to the bride's parents to a crowning in church and a plate broken at the groom's door.

Our new guide follows Armenian wedding traditions in the order families live them, and is plain about which details come from UNESCO, the Smithsonian or parish sources and which are simply often told.

Inside: khosk-kap, the kavor and kavorkin, the crowns and the shared cup, lavash and honey at the door, the duduk and Kochari, plus how Armenian-Australian couples keep the customs at home.

Thinking of marrying in Armenia itself? The guide also covers the current Smartraveller advice and the questions to ask the registry and the embassy before you set a date.

Which custom matters most to your family? Tell us in the comments, or start a conversation with a Wedded Advisor through the link in our bio.
